anchors.exact: Constructed entirely from standard ConvNet modules, ConvNeXts compete favorably with Transformers in terms of accuracy and scalability, achieving 87.8% ImageNet top-1 accuracy and outperforming Swin Transformers on COCO detection and ADE20K segmentation, while maintaining the simplicity and efficiency of standard ConvNets.
Surprisingly, ConvNeXts, constructed entirely from standard ConvNet modules, compete favorably with Transformers in terms of accuracy, scalability and robustness across all major benchmarks.

We propose ConvNeXts, a pure ConvNet model that can compete favorably with state-of-the-art hierarchical vision Transformers across multiple computer vision benchmarks, while retaining the simplicity and efficiency of standard ConvNets.

nodes.flag: The abstract says ConvNeXt is 'outperforming Swin Transformers on COCO detection and ADE20K segmentation', but the results section itself describes the ImageNet-1K-pretrained COCO rows as 'on-par or better' (e.g. 50.4 vs 50.4 box AP for Swin-T under Cascade Mask-RCNN). The comparators are specifically Swin, DeiT and ViT trained on ImageNet-1K/22K; 'Transformers' in general and larger-scale data regimes are not tested.
nodes.label: ConvNeXts, built entirely from standard ConvNet modules, compete favorably with hierarchical vision Transformers in accuracy and scalability across classification, detection and segmentation while keeping the simplicity and efficiency of standard ConvNets.
nodes.note: Code is released at https://github.com/facebookresearch/ConvNeXt (b3), so the training and evaluation could in principle be re-run.
nodes.short: Pure ConvNet matches Transformers across benchmarks

anchors.exact: We gradually “modernize” a standard ResNet toward the design of a vision Transformer, and discover several key components that contribute to the performance difference along the way.
Many Transformer architectural choices can be incorporated in a ConvNet, and they lead to increasingly better performance.
Intriguingly, a significant portion of the design choices taken in a vision Transformer may be mapped to ConvNet instantiations.

nodes.flag: The roadmap is a single greedy path in a fixed order: each modification is tested only on top of all previous ones, and not every step increases accuracy (depthwise conv drops to 78.28, moving up the depthwise conv drops to 79.92 in Table 10). No ablation removes individual components from the final model, so the per-component contributions reported are order-dependent and a different ordering could attribute gains differently.
nodes.label: Many architectural choices from vision Transformers can be incorporated into a plain ConvNet, and a ResNet gradually 'modernized' along this roadmap reaches increasingly better ImageNet-1K performance.
nodes.note: The source states in §2.6 closing remarks that none of the design choices are novel in the ConvNet literature; the contribution claimed is their collective application.
nodes.short: Transformer design choices transfer to ConvNets

anchors.exact: implying that a significant portion of the performance difference between traditional ConvNets and vision
Transformers may be due to the training techniques.

nodes.flag: The inference rests on one architecture (ResNet-50) and one recipe change (+2.7%). The source does not show how much of the ResNet-50 vs Swin-T gap (78.8 vs 81.3 after the recipe) is closed for other ConvNets, so 'a significant portion' is a generalization from a single model, though it is hedged with 'may'.
nodes.label: A significant portion of the performance gap between traditional ConvNets and vision Transformers may be due to training techniques rather than architecture.
nodes.short: Training recipe explains much of gap

anchors.exact: Additionally, we observe that the benefit of larger kernel sizes reaches a saturation point at 7×7.
The network’s performance increases from 79.9% (3×3) to 80.6% (7×7), while the network’s FLOPs stay roughly the same.

nodes.label: Enlarging the depthwise kernel raises accuracy at roughly constant FLOPs, with the benefit saturating at 7×7.
nodes.note: In Table 10 the 7×7 and 9×9 results are identical (80.57) with overlapping standard deviations, and 5×5 is 80.35; the differences between 5, 7 and 9 are within about two standard deviations. Appendix C reports saturation at 5×5 rather than 7×7 in the ResNet-200 regime.

anchors.exact: We can improve the accuracy to 82.0%, significantly exceeding Swin-T’s 81.3%.
discovered ConvNeXt, a pure ConvNet, that can outperform the Swin Transformer for ImageNet-1K classification in this compute regime.

anchors.exact: We observe ConvNeXt can perform generally on par with ViT, showing that our ConvNeXt block design is competitive when used in non-hierarchical models.

anchors.exact: Across different model complexities, ConvNeXt achieves on-par or better performance than Swin Transformer.
in many cases ConvNeXt is significantly better (e.g. +1.0 AP) than Swin Transformers in terms of box and mask AP.

nodes.flag: ConvNeXt COCO results come from a hyper-parameter sweep over learning rate, layer-wise decay and stochastic depth (b285), whereas ImageNet-1K-pretrained Swin numbers are taken from the Swin GitHub repository. The source states the same sweep was applied only to ImageNet-22K-pretrained Swin-B/L, so the 1K-regime comparisons involve unequal tuning effort. Single runs without variance are reported, so differences of 0.1–0.2 AP cannot be distinguished from noise.
nodes.label: On COCO detection and instance segmentation, ConvNeXt is on par with or better than Swin at every model size, and with ImageNet-22K pre-training is often significantly better (about +1.0 AP).
nodes.short: ConvNeXt matches or beats Swin on COCO
nodes.where: §4 Object detection and segmentation on COCO

anchors.exact: ConvNeXt models can achieve competitive performance across different model capacities, further validating the effectiveness of our architecture design.

nodes.label: On ADE20K semantic segmentation, ConvNeXt backbones achieve competitive mIoU across model capacities.
nodes.note: Swin numbers are cited from the Swin repository; ConvNeXt results use a small hyper-parameter sweep (b286) and multi-scale testing following Swin.

anchors.exact: the inference throughputs of ConvNeXts are comparable to or exceed that of Swin Transformers.
we notice that training ConvNeXts requires less memory than training Swin Transformers.
ConvNeXts’ advantage is now significantly greater, sometimes up to 49% faster.

nodes.flag: The training-memory statement is supported by a single example (ConvNeXt-B vs Swin-B in Cascade Mask-RCNN, 17.4 vs 18.5 GB) yet is phrased for ConvNeXts in general; no memory figures are given for other sizes or for classification training. The A100 study is described by the source itself as preliminary and uses a channels-last layout that benefits convolutions; it is unclear whether Swin was run with equivalent optimizations.
nodes.label: Despite depthwise convolutions, ConvNeXt is practically efficient: its inference throughput matches or exceeds Swin's, it trains with less memory, and on A100 GPUs it is up to 49% faster.
nodes.short: ConvNeXt is practically efficient in deployment
nodes.where: §4 Remarks on model efficiency; Appendix E

nodes.flag: At the tiny scale, RVT-S is better than ConvNeXt-T on every robustness column in Table 8 (e.g. mCE 49.4 vs 53.2, ImageNet-A 25.7 vs 24.2); the advantage appears only at the base scale on A/R/Sketch. nodes.note: The recipe is held fixed while architecture changes, so hyper-parameters tuned for the starting ResNet or for Swin may favor some intermediate steps over others; the source does not re-tune per step.

We train ConvNeXts for 300 epochs using AdamW [46] with a learning rate of 4e-3.
